Alternatively, this location corresponds anatomically to the **medial patellar retinaculum** or **medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) insertion zone on the medial patellar border/tibia**, but tenderness there would usually be more anterior/superficial and associated with patellar instability—yet she has no history of subluxation, negative instability tests, and full ROM without pain. Given her obesity, PCOS, and sudden increase in activity, **pes anserine bursitis/tendinopathy** is highly plausible: it is common in overweight individuals due to increased Q-angle and valgus stress, presents with insidious or acute-onset medial knee pain without swelling or instability, and localizes to the medial proximal tibia—often described as “below the kneecap”. MRI is not required for diagnosis; clinical diagnosis is sufficient when findings align. Other considerations (e.g., early osteoarthritis) are unlikely in a 23-year-old without prior injury or systemic inflammation. Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) typically causes anterior or retropatellar pain, not discrete tibial tenderness. Thus, the most consistent diagnosis is pes anserine bursitis.

DIAGNOSIS: Pes anserine bursitis
